**Project name:** COURTSIDE

**Tagline:** Who gets paid in the seconds after a tennis point, and what it takes to be first.

**Team:** Ojasva Mishra, Yoan Exposito, Rafael Penhas, Ian Hoang (University of Florida)

**Track:** Systematic Trading

## Inspiration
In-play tennis markets on Polymarket jump at every point. We asked a trader's question: when the price moves, who is
on the other side, and why do they lose? Tennis has a clean information ladder. Ball tracking sees the result before
the ball lands, the umpire logs it seconds later, data feeds follow, and public streams and score pages
trail by tens of seconds. That makes it a natural lab for pricing speed.

## What it does
- **Maps who makes money after each point**, on 13,084 resolved ATP/WTA/Challenger moneylines
  ($2.84B traded, Oct 8, 2025 to Oct 3, 2026), from Polymarket's public trade tapes. Every print is
  classified by side, and every fee is the match's own.
- **Finds a persistent fast tier.** Wallets that trade within 3 s of a score move, chosen walk-forward on past months,
  earn +0.93¢ / +0.67¢ a share after fees (in sample / held out, OOS prints only) and are positive in
  9/9 in-sample and 3/3 out-of-sample months. Other takers lose, and copying the same trades
  3 s later loses.
- **Turns that edge into a frozen book, v2,** measured at the fast tier's own fills (the opportunity at their speed,
  not our execution). In sample: Sharpe 14.5 [11.9, 17.4], +1.38¢ a share, max drawdown −2.0%,
  deflated Sharpe 0.997. On the held-out window, which is burned for v2 (non-blind: v2 was designed after v1
  finished at −$36,056 there): Sharpe 6.7 [1.9, 12.3], +0.60¢ [0.09, 1.13], deflated Sharpe
  0.075, and **negative when fees double** (−0.34¢). On 11,307 never-examined markets its
  blind out-of-sample test failed (+1.22¢ [−0.19, 2.65]).
- **Blind forward test:** pre-registered but not run within the hackathon window (HYPOTHESIS_V2.md A5).
- **Prices the speed a computer-vision trader needs**, in simulation: the feed latency is assumed (we bought no
  licensed feed and have no match video); the other parameters are measured. Pre-registered, its **break-even feed delay
  is 1.0–1.1 s**. At the 1 s base case it makes +$4 a day held out
  (−0.38¢ a share): the call must reach the venue 0.89 s before the umpire's stamp.
  At 0.5 / 1 / 3 s it makes +$15 / +$4 / −$13 a day held out. A post
  hoc estimate of the umpire's lag (3.14 s, assumes courtside humans) gives +$94 a day in
  sample (Sharpe 11.9) and +$57 held out (Sharpe 8.8) at 1 s. The same
  clocks read point by point give −$17 a day, and a replay on 9 real recorded books, calling
  every point ex ante, loses in 36 of 36 settings. The simulated trade set is points that
  later moved ≥ 4¢ (selected on outcomes, not ex ante), so it is an upper bound. We claim a price on each second of
  speed, not a bankable CV P&L.
- **Proves the pipeline is fast enough.** Our own path, video frame to unsigned paper order, takes 54 ms
  (p50 of 24 traces). With a simulated 1 s feed, 65 ms of network and Polymarket's 1 s order hold, the
  order is executable at 2,119 ms, under the organisers' 3 s bar. No order was sent.
- **Calls table-tennis points before the ball lands.** On real held-out table-tennis footage, our live causal vision
  engine called 4 of 41 misses before contact, none wrong (median lead 162 ms), at
  119.9 fps on one L4 GPU, 4.6 ms p50 per frame to call-ready (the video's 6.9 ms is the
  p50 per emitted call), 0 frames dropped. (The offline evaluation's 11 of
  11 used a look-ahead feature, so we lead with the live engine.) For tennis, a spin-aware tracker cuts
  landing error from 5.76 to 0.57 cm at 200 ms before the bounce in simulated physics; our
  tennis calls are simulated, and the video's real rally (licensed stock footage) shows only the tracked ball trail (public detector, our linking).
- **Measures latency live.** The book reprices 1.2 s before the official point stamp; ESPN,
  Polymarket's own sports feed and the WTA API trail the book by 28.2–44.1 s.

## How we built it
Python on public Polymarket and Kalshi APIs (no keys); an exact point-level tennis Markov model for fair value and point
leverage; a websocket recorder for live order books and four score feeds; a replay engine that makes paper orders wait
the venue's delay plus our measured network latency, then walk the recorded book; a causal ball-tracking and call
engine (BlurBall detector, our tracker and a frozen point-end classifier) running on HiPerGator L4 GPUs and streamed
over WebRTC; a latency sweep of 18,880 simulation runs; and a six-lens optimisation workflow in which every claimed
improvement was attacked by two independent verifier agents before it could enter v2. The paper is LaTeX, built by a
script that reads every number from a results file and records its source in `results/paper/numbers.json`. We wrote
the code during the event with AI coding assistants.

## Challenges we ran into
Being honest with ourselves. v1 finished at −$36,056 on the held-out window. A verifier caught hindsight in our first v2
draft (an onset look-ahead); fixing it cut in-sample Sharpe from 16.8 to 14.5. Our first vision
numbers came from an offline evaluation with a look-ahead feature; the live causal engine calls fewer misses, and that
is the number we report. The stamp lag, the one number that decides the CV P&L, cannot be measured without a licensed
feed, so we show both readings and lead with the pre-registered one. Every blind or ex-ante test of a tradable book
failed, and all of them are in the paper. (The video's "2 pass · 4 fail" also
counts two blind tests that are not tradable books: the table-tennis call precision and v2's unseen markets in sample.)

## Accomplishments that we're proud of
- A wallet-level map of the latency tier in a live prediction market, and a dollar price on each second of feed delay.
- A frame-to-order pipeline measured stage by stage: 54 ms of our own time against a 3 s budget.
- A vision engine that calls misses before contact on footage it never saw, at 119.9 fps.
- Discipline: hypotheses committed before results, 4,219 variants counted in all (3,410 strategy
  variants, the video's count; 3,386 in the deflated Sharpe), 111 reads of held-out data logged and
  classified, deflated Sharpe, PBO, block bootstrap, blind tests on 11,307 unseen markets, and every failure
  reported.

## What we learned
In today's regime (1 s order hold, 5% fee, ~131 competing fast wallets) the edge is real but, out
of sample, smaller than one price tick (+0.60¢ a share), and it does not survive doubled costs. It pays only whoever reaches the
stale quote first, and public data is the slow tier. Our own pipeline is not the bottleneck: the venue holds every
order for a second. The binding constraints are a licensed sub-second feed, the unmeasured lag from bounce to umpire
stamp, and capacity, which is small: v2's held-out edge holds only up to 1× size ($22,754), and the CV
book's post hoc Sharpe halves at $40,000 of capital held out.

## What's next for COURTSIDE
- Run the pre-registered blind forward test, which we did not run within the hackathon window, and report it
  whatever it says.
- One session with a licensed low-latency feed and test orders to measure the stamp lag and whether delayed orders are
  released on a 1 s clock. That single number moves the break-even one for one.
- Evaluate the coded rally-state gate against phantom calls outside play, and move the vision engine to tennis video.
- With a licensed feed, the measured stamp lag decides whether there is anything to deploy; the engine, its risk limits
  and kill switches are already in code. Until then, COURTSIDE prices speed; it is not yet a business.

## Pre-existing components (disclosed per Participant Terms §14.2)
- BlurBall pretrained table-tennis ball-detector weights and model code (Gossard et al., MIT licence), built on WASB-SBDT
  (Tarashima et al., MIT), used zero-shot.
- TrackNet ball-detector weights and TennisProject / TennisCourtDetector code (yastrebksv; no licence file), used
  unmodified for evaluation and not redistributed.
- Public datasets: OpenTTGames (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), the TrackNet tennis dataset, the Kenneth R. French Data Library factors.
- In the video: a licensed stock tennis clip, “Tennis Players Playing Match” by Gelato Prod, Pexels (Pexels License), shown with the tracked ball trail (public TrackNet detector, our linking) (not a
  match we traded); narration and music bed generated with ElevenLabs (AI voice).
- Open-source Python libraries listed in `requirements.txt` and `requirements-extra.txt`.
